sentences.text: The meeting focused on conceptual design for a new TV remote control, with participants discussing design features, user needs, and technical constraints. The group agreed to adopt a flip-top or shell-like design to improve usability and reduce repetitive strain, and to exclude voice recognition and

Market research indicated that users prioritize a fashionable appearance over ease of use, with 75% finding current remotes ugly and 80% willing to pay more for a stylish remote. The team also confirmed that the remote will be limited to TV functions only, excluding video programming and teletext.

Participants discussed battery options, with standard double A or triple A batteries identified as the most practical and cost-effective, while solar and kinetic charging were considered but deemed less viable due to cost, durability, and limited real-world applicability.

Participant A proposed a flip-open design to reduce control size and introduce an electronic panel for programming, emphasizing that the product should be accessible to a wide age range and reflect the company's image through fashion in electronics.

Participant B reported market research findings indicating that 75% of users find current remote controls ugly and 80% would pay more for a fancy design; additionally, 75% 'zap' frequently, and 50% only use 10% of the buttons, suggesting a need for simplicity and visual appeal.

Participant B stated that the most important feature for users is fashion, followed by technological innovation, with ease of use being the least important—despite being a key factor in user experience.

Participant C proposed a flip-top remote with main functions on the top and complex functions in the middle, advocating for user-friendliness and simplicity, noting that 30–40% of users do not use 30–40% of the buttons on current remotes.

Participant D presented a working design concept using infrared signals to send commands such as power, channel, or volume, with a decoder chip converting inputs and a wireless range of up to five meters, though the design is not confirmed to work and is considered a basic idea.

Participant D suggested that the remote should be small, easy to carry, and easy to lose, and proposed a feature to prevent loss—such as a way to go down the side of the sofa—while acknowledging that the design must conform to the TV's existing infrared protocol.
Participant B acknowledged that the remote being easy to lose is a significant issue, citing market research that 50% of users report losing remotes and 34% take too long to learn how to use them.

Participant A emphasized that the remote should not have a bulky or insignificant form factor, and suggested large rubber buttons or a touch screen panel to improve usability and reduce wear, with touch screens appealing to younger, office-based users.

Participant B expressed concern about repetitive strain injury (RSI) from small movements on a touch screen, suggesting that RSI may need to be postponed to a future meeting, while noting that a flip-top or curved design could reduce thumb strain.
Participant B stated that the team will not include teletext or video programming, as users consider them outdated, and that the product will only be for TV use to simplify design and reduce cost.
The group agreed to adopt a flip-top or shell-like design as a primary form factor, with a curved, semi-circular shape to reduce thumb pressure and improve grip.
The remote control will be limited to TV functions only, excluding video programming, teletext, and combined TV-video control features.
The design will prioritize a fashionable, trendy appearance to appeal to users, with the product incorporating company branding such as a logo and a modern, stylish aesthetic.
The group decided to exclude voice recognition from the design due to high cost and low effectiveness, as noted in market research and technical feasibility assessments.
The remote will use standard double A or triple A batteries as the primary power source, as they are cost-effective, widely available, and practical for the device’s function.
Participant D to present the remote control design concept, including circuit details and signal transmission, with a follow-up presentation on battery and power options.
Participant B to conduct a market research review and provide a summary of user preferences, particularly regarding design, functionality, and age group appeal, with a focus on fashion and usability.

Participant C to evaluate the flip-top design concept and propose a set of five to six design variations with different appearances (e.g., psychedelic, sleek) to test appeal across age groups and markets.
Participant A to lead the design process from the inside out, focusing on core functionality and circuitry before expanding to external form and user interface.

Participant D to confirm that the remote will not include voice recognition, and to document the technical rationale for excluding solar and kinetic charging options due to cost, durability, and limited real-world viability.
